questions.question: The point (−3,4) lies in:
solutionSteps: Its x-coordinate is negative and y-coordinate positive.
This sign combination identifies Quadrant II.

questions.question: The distance between (1,2) and (4,6) is:
solutionSteps: The horizontal and vertical changes are 3 and 4.

questions.question: Explain how assigning coordinates to a geometric point connects geometry with algebra. On a grid, mark A(2,1) and B(−1,3), and describe B relative to A.
questions.finalAnswer: B is 3 units left and 2 units above A; coordinates allow geometric properties to be expressed algebraically.
solutionSteps: Two perpendicular axes and a common origin fix the reference system.
An ordered pair records signed horizontal and vertical displacements; equations can then describe sets of geometric points.
B − A = (−1 − 2, 3 − 1) = (−3,2). Plot using these displacements.

questions.question: Find the midpoint of A(−2,5) and B(6,−1). Verify it by comparing the displacements from each endpoint.
solutionSteps: M − A = (4,−3) and B − M = (4,−3), so M is equally placed along the segment.

questions.question: A rectangular classroom has grid vertices (0,0), (8,0), (8,6), (0,6), with 1 grid unit = 1 metre. Mark the centre and find the straight-line distance from (0,0) to the opposite corner.
solutionSteps: Draw a rectangle 8 units wide and 6 units high using the given coordinates.
The centre is the midpoint of opposite corners: ((0 + 8)/2, (0 + 6)/2) = (4,3).

questions.question: Use distances to decide whether A(0,0), B(2,2) and C(5,5) are collinear.
questions.finalAnswer: They are collinear, with B between A and C.
solutionSteps: AB + BC = AC, so equality in the triangle inequality places B on segment AC.

questions.question: Check whether A(0,0), B(4,0), C(0,3) form a right-angled triangle. Identify the right-angle vertex.
questions.finalAnswer: The triangle is right-angled at A.
solutionSteps: AB² + AC² = BC²; by the converse of Pythagoras the angle opposite BC, at A, is 90°.
